vulnerabilities.description: Code injection pattern detection using simple regex. The pattern `/\beval\b|\bnew\s+Function\b|\$\{|`/` may not catch all code injection variants (e.g., 'eval ' with extra spaces, or using Function constructor indirectly). This is adequate as defense-in-depth but not foolproof.

Arbitrary recursion depth limit of 4 levels in validateContextValue(). Values nested beyond 4 levels are rejected, which could cause unexpected validation failures for deeply nested legitimate data structures.

Key file permissions verified on read, but no integrity/MAC verification of the key file itself. If permissions are compromised by an attacker with system access, the key could be read or tampered with before validation occurs.

Shell metacharacter check skips flag values entirely (as noted: 'skip shell-meta check for flag VALUES'). While this is safe due to file piping, a flag injection attack through crafted titles/bodies could theoretically occur if the piping mechanism fails.

recommendations: Upgrade code injection detection in session.js from simple regex to an AST-based approach or use a dedicated code-detection library for eval/Function patterns
Remove or increase the arbitrary recursion depth limit in validateContextValue() - allow deeper nesting or document why depth 4 is required
Add periodic key rotation mechanism using the keyVersion field in the encryption envelope for long-running sessions
Implement HMAC verification for key files to detect tampering on read (in addition to permission checks)
Add security headers and CSP validation if these helper scripts are exposed to any web context
Audit the webpack/build artifact files (.sst/platform, docs/plans) - many appear to be minified third-party code; ensure dependency versions are current and free of known CVEs
Document the threat model for the helpers (what attacks they defend against vs. what's out of scope)
Consider adding rate limiting to shell command execution in github-safe.js to prevent resource exhaustion
